newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. chief to signal start of Iraqi oil plan.
newsitem.headline: U.N. chief to signal start of Iraqi oil plan.

text.p: Barring last minute obstacles, U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali is ready to give the go-ahead for the Iraqi oil-for-food plan on Monday, U.N. officials said.
"It will happen on Monday," said one senior envoy on Sunday, in reference to a report Boutros-Ghali must give the Security Council certifying that the programme was ready to be implemented.

Under an agreement Iraq accepted on May 20, Baghdad can begin to sell oil for the first time since August 1990 when U.N. trade sanctions were imposed in response to President Saddam Hussein's invasion of Kuwait.
The deal allows Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil every six months for the purchase of badly-needed food, medicine and other necessities for its people, suffering under the embargoes.

UNICEF, the U.N. Children's Fund, has estimated 4,500 children under five years of age are dying each month from hunger and disease. And the U.N. World Food Programmes says about 180,000 children under five are malnourished.

Of the $2 billion, about two-thirds will go to Iraq for humanitarian goods under a tightly-monitored programme. The remainder is to go to a compensation fund for Gulf War victims and U.N. costs to rid Iraq of weapons of mass destruction.

If Boutros-Ghali delivers his one-page report to the council on Monday, the plan is can be implemented officially a minute after midnight EST (0500 GMT) on Tuesday, according to a 1995 Security Council resolution that sets out terms for the deal.

Iraq's oil minister, Gen. Amir Muhammad Rasheed, said oil exports would begin on Tuesday. But U.N. spokeswoman Sylvana Foa doubted that would be the case, noting that New York-based oil experts or overseers had up to 24 hours to review all contracts.

On Friday, the last technical obstacle was resolved when inspectors from the Netherlands-based Saybolt firm hired by the United Nations said that Iraq's pipeline to Turkey was now functioning properly.
Foa said the experts reported that key metering equipment at Iraq's Zakho station along its border with Turkey, through which the bulk of the oil will pass, was in working order.
Before invading Kuwait in 1990, Iraq exported more than 3 million barrels per day (bpd). At current world oil prices, Baghdad would be allowed to export slightly under 600,000 bpd.

Iraq and the United Nations signed the terms for the oil-for-food deal on May 20, after months of negotiations and U.S. insistence on at least 150 U.N. monitors in the field to make sure humanitarian goods were distributed equitably.
The plan was then ready to be implemented in September but Boutros-Ghali suspended it after Iraq sent troops into an international protected area for Kurds in the north.
Baghdad then balked at the number and composition of the U.N. food monitoring teams and insisted that the United States endorse an oil-pricing formula crucial to carrying out the deal.

Washington had delayed in approving the formula that all other council members accepted. Its allies speculated that President Bill Clinton wanted to make sure no action was taken during his presidential campaign that could be construed as helping Saddam.
However, all political obstacles were removed on Nov. 25, when Iraq dropped its demands and the United States said it would not stand in the way of the deal going ahead.
